en: Sādhanamālā 248 [= Tōh. 1627] Mahāmāyāsādhana (author unknown) [NGMPP B 24/12, DSCN9071 = 952 ff.]
Having paid homage to Vajraḍāka, the Victorious One whose nature is Mahāmāyā,
the sequence of his sādhana is here set forth in accordance with the oral tradition.
Faithful, through the application of loving-kindness and compassion, having set his mind upon perfect enlightenment,
endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth, and possessing an even disposition regarding the eight worldly concerns;
One who knows the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of mantra, tantra, and so forth,
being seated comfortably in a place suitable for proper conduct, should place the syllable *HŪṂ* upon the sun at his heart.
Having worshipped with offerings arising from that light, and having fixed one's mind before it,
one should then cultivate emptiness after performing the confession of misdeeds and so forth.
One should recite mentally: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness."
In the sky, upon a red four-petaled lotus situated within a solar disc,
one should meditate on five white drops that perform the functions of emanation and reabsorption.
One should contemplate that the four ḍākinīs, who have arisen from the drops at the four directions, are dancing and eager for union;
they possess the very nature of great loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth, practiced previously,
and they are impelling [the practitioner].
O friend, the lotus of the heart has blossomed by the drum;
alas, alas! it has been propitiated through great bliss by means of dance.
The lotus, opened wide by the rays of the sun, [shines] with great bliss.
Then, with the intention of uplifting sentient beings from the sufferings of saṃsāra,
he beheld the reality of the world as it truly is— like an illusion—
and [visualized] the blue syllable *hūṃ*, born from the central drop, consisting of compassion.
Beautiful with the supreme bliss of his own nature consisting of the five wisdoms and three bodies,
he has four faces and four arms, and his body is smeared with ashes.
His root body is blue, while his right face is yellow.
Behind him is one with a white and red luster, and to the left one brilliant with emerald;
he has three eyes, is adorned with the five mudrās such as the human skin,
has tawny hair standing erect with Akṣobhya at its crown, and is formidable with a skull-diadem.
Holding a skull-cup in his right hand and a khaṭvāṅga staff and bow in his left,
he has performed the welfare of the world through various Buddhas flashing like ten million rays of light;
he is embraced by his own Buddha-Ḍākinī during the festival of passion.
One should meditate on Heruka dancing, his face gazed upon by the four goddesses;
the symbols and so forth of the ḍākinīs in the four directions are now described.
There, on the eastern petal, is Vajraḍākinī, blue in color,
with four faces— blue, yellow, white, red, and green—
and [holding] a vajra and a skull-cup, purified by the earth element and the mirror-like gnosis (ādarśajñāna).
In her left hands she holds a bell and a khaṭvāṅga;
in her right hands she holds the waters of the element of the knowledge of equanimity.
Śrī Ratnaḍākinī has a mass of jewels and a trident in her hands.
On the left, she has a jackal with its neck pressed down as her excellent banner;
she has four faces of yellow, blue, white, red, and greenish-yellow luster.
On the western petal, however, is Padma-Ḍākinī, who is white and reddish.
She may be a young woman whose nature consists of the contemplation of fire and so forth.
Her faces resemble white, reddish, molten gold, blue, and green;
she holds a universal lotus and an arrow in her right hands, and a skull-cup and a bow in the others.

In the north is Viśvaḍākinī, whose faces are green, yellow, white, red, and black; she is the purification of the [deeds] performed (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna), the wind element, and so forth. She holds a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaru in her right hands, and a noose and a skull-cup in her left hands.
All the goddesses have three eyes and four faces, and all possess four arms.
They are immersed in the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra), radiant with the [auspicious] marks and signs,
seated upon fierce postures (raudrāsana), and dancing like their lords, adorned with finger-rings and other ornaments.
One should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgavinyāsa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Lord,
the consecration by the Victors (*jinābhiṣeka*), worship, praise, and acts of devotion, and so forth;
one should then place [the mantras] on the forehead, the throat, the eyes, the ears, the nose, and the heart.
Oṃ āḥ a khecira; thus, after the letter *ra*, there is the syllable *hūṃ*.
Having summoned the wisdom maṇḍala through the union of the vajra-clap,
and having caused it to enter preceded by the offering of water for the feet and so forth, one should personally effect their unification.
Together with the wheel of commitments (samayacakra), for the sake of attaining the distinguished fruit,
[it occurs] through the entry of the essence (rasa), just as copper and other metals achieve the state of silver.
Having exhorted the Protectors situated in the directions by means of the heart-flame residing in his own heart,
[he should perform the rite] with the vidyās arising from their radiance and with jars filled with the water of nectar.
From the consecration by the Lord, Akṣobhya [appears] upon the head of the divine women;
furthermore, Vairocana, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi [appear],
with their hands occupied in performing excellent worship through goddesses emanated from meditative absorption.
One should worship oneself as Heruka, joined with the Yoginīs, and offer praise.
"I bow to Śrī Heruka, who is adorned with a garland of mantras and a necklace of large, formidable fangs, and who is devouring great quantities of flesh"—
thus ends the song of praise.
One should meditate on the seed-syllables OṂ HŪṂ SVĀ ĀḤ HĀ in sequence upon the head, heart, navel, secret place, and the pair of thighs, [visualizing her] as consisting of the five families;
she whose secret lotus is red with the syllable HRĪḤ and whose pericarp is yellow with the syllable BHRŪṂ.
Beholding his own consort, the illustrious Buddha-Ḍākinī, who is red and eager for the joy of passion,
he is exhorted by song by the four noble goddesses.
"Oṃ! I, the Vajra of the Born-Jewel, with *hūṃ* and through various acts of making [her] rejoice, shall cause the Jinas to be impassioned"—with such thoughts of passion, he should begin.
Having summoned [the goddesses] with the sounds of *phaṭ* from the clashing of the vajra and lotus, they are caused to enter through his mouth.
Through the immersion in bliss, the host of Jinas swiftly emerges from the vajra;
having tasted the true mind in the lotus according to the ritual with the tongue,
[one should place it] upon the four-petaled red lotus of the heart, which is the nature of the four elements.
The bindu situated in the sun is encapsulated and well-enveloped by the moon; it is reached by lines resembling lotus fibers, numbering six and a half,
which form rows of syllables.
Having emitted the sound from there upwards, one should cause it to enter the aperture of the moon; thus there shall be the going and coming.
While pronouncing it, one should emit the mantra-illusion along with the vital breaths without withdrawing it;
likewise, one should perform the entry and exit of the resonance (nāda) through the three syllables. When the wind moves upward and exits, the sound of the three syllables issues forth.
When [the breath] enters, it enters;

when it stays, it stays within the subtle black drop (*asitabindu*) in the wind. Thus, the knots, vowels, and consonants consist of entry, staying, and exit along seven and a half lines of energy (*guṇarekhā*).
One should meditate with a mind whose movement has been brought to a very gentle state and turned away from other objects.
"Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ" is the mantra for the recitation of the three syllables.
When desiring to rise, one should perform worship and the like, and look upon those who are suffering.
One who is liberated through the vision of the reality of the world should dedicate their merit for the welfare of others.
By whatever merit has been accumulated through the meditation on Vajraḍāka,
may I become Vajraḍāka for the sake of attaining the state of the Lord of the World.
Having arisen, one whose form is that of Heruka for oneself and others should perform activities such as collecting alms and explaining the teachings, like a master of illusion.
The food, consecrated by the syllable *hūṃ*, resides within a skull-cup born from the syllable *āḥ*.
Blazing from below by the wheel of wind and fire, it is purified. Above, having visualized the syllable *oṃ*, one empowers it through recitation so that it becomes nectar.
One should satisfy [the deity] with this, drawn through the nozzle of the tongue-vajra ray.
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ, O you who consume the secret [substance], I shall consume it—this is the mantra for tasting the nectar.
As before, at the time of bathing, one should perform the ritual of consecration;
in this manner, one should meditate briefly during all four junctions of the day.
By whatever merit I have gained from composing this *Sādhana* of Vajraḍāka,
may all people today become adorned with the pride of that [realization].
The *Herukasādhanopāyikā* according to the *Mahāmāyā Tantra* is completed.
